title: Equilibrium, Acids & Bases
description: K expressions, Q vs K, Le Chatelier, Kp vs Kc, Kw and pH, strong acids, Ka·Kb, Lewis acids, buffers, half-equivalence, Ksp and the common-ion effect.

cards.title: Write $K_c$ for $\ce{CaCO3(s) <=> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$.
cards.body:
$K_c = [\ce{CO2}]$

Pure solids and pure liquids are left out of $K$: their activity is **1**.

Likewise $K_p = P_{\ce{CO2}}$, so at a given temperature the $\ce{CO2}$ pressure is fixed no matter how much solid is present.

Why: a solid's concentration is fixed by its density, so it can't change as the reaction proceeds.
Watch out: some solid must be present, or the system can't be at equilibrium.
cards.searchQuery: equilibrium constant expression pure solids excluded CaCO3

cards.title: A reaction mixture has $Q < K$. In which direction does the reaction proceed to reach equilibrium?
cards.body:
Forward (to the right)

Products form until $Q$ rises to equal $K$.

$Q$ has the same form as $K$ but uses the **current** concentrations. If $Q > K$ the reaction runs in reverse; if $Q = K$ it is already at equilibrium.

Mnemonic: $Q$ is smaller than $K$, so the mixture needs more of the numerator: more products.
cards.searchQuery: reaction quotient Q less than K direction of shift

cards.title: $\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g)}$ is at equilibrium. Which way does it shift when the container volume is decreased?
cards.body:
To the right, toward $\ce{NH3}$

There are 2 mol of gas on the right and 4 mol on the left. Compression raises the pressure, and the system relieves it by making **fewer gas molecules**.

$K$ stays the same; only the position of equilibrium moves.

Watch out: adding an inert gas at constant volume causes no shift, because the partial pressures don't change.
cards.searchQuery: Le Chatelier volume decrease Haber process shift right

cards.title: Which kind of change alters the numerical value of an equilibrium constant $K$?
cards.body:
A change in temperature

For a given balanced equation, nothing else changes $K$. Concentration, pressure or volume changes shift the position ($Q \ne K$) but leave $K$ alone, and a catalyst speeds both directions equally.

Raising $T$ **lowers** $K$ for an exothermic reaction and **raises** it for an endothermic one.

Key idea: only temperature changes $K$.
cards.searchQuery: what changes equilibrium constant temperature only

cards.title: In $K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n}$, what is $\Delta n$ for $\ce{PCl5(g) <=> PCl3(g) + Cl2(g)}$?
cards.body:
+1

$\Delta n$ is moles of **gaseous** products minus moles of gaseous reactants: $2 - 1 = +1$.

Use $R = 0.08206\,\mathrm{L\,atm/(mol\,K)}$ and $T$ in kelvin.

Example: for $\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$, $\Delta n = 0$, so $K_p = K_c$.
cards.searchQuery: Kp Kc relationship delta n gaseous moles

cards.title: Name the six common strong acids.
cards.body:
$\ce{HCl}$, $\ce{HBr}$, $\ce{HI}$, $\ce{HNO3}$, $\ce{HClO4}$ and $\ce{H2SO4}$ (first proton only)

They ionize essentially **100%** in water, so for a monoprotic strong acid $[\ce{H3O+}]$ equals the acid concentration.

Watch out: $\ce{HF}$ is a **weak** acid despite fluorine's electronegativity; the $\ce{H-F}$ bond is very strong.
cards.searchQuery: six common strong acids list HCl HBr HI HNO3 HClO4 H2SO4

cards.title: What is the value of $K_w$, the ion-product constant of water, at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$?
cards.body:
$K_w = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}$

$K_w = [\ce{H3O+}][\ce{OH-}]$. In pure water both equal $1.0 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{M}$, so neutral pH is 7.00.

Water's autoionization is endothermic, so $K_w$ grows with temperature.

Watch out: at $50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ neutral pH is about 6.6, yet the water is still **neutral** because $[\ce{H3O+}] = [\ce{OH-}]$.
cards.searchQuery: Kw ion product of water 1.0 x 10^-14 at 25 C

cards.title: At $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ a solution has $[\ce{OH-}] = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{M}$. What is its pH, to two decimal places?
cards.body:
10.00

$\mathrm{pOH} = -\log(1.0 \times 10^{-4}) = 4.00$, and $\mathrm{pH} + \mathrm{pOH} = 14.00$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Equivalently, $[\ce{H3O+}] = K_w/[\ce{OH-}] = 1.0 \times 10^{-10}\,\mathrm{M}$.

Watch out: 4.00 is the **pOH**, not the pH.
cards.searchQuery: calculate pH from hydroxide concentration pOH

cards.title: Acetic acid has $K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$. What is $K_b$ for its conjugate base, acetate ($\ce{CH3COO-}$), at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$? Give two significant figures.
cards.body:
$K_b = 5.6 \times 10^{-10}$

For any conjugate acid-base pair, $K_aK_b = K_w = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}$, so $K_b = (1.0 \times 10^{-14})/(1.8 \times 10^{-5})$.

Equivalently, $\mathrm{p}K_a + \mathrm{p}K_b = 14.00$.

Key idea: the **stronger** the acid, the **weaker** its conjugate base.
cards.searchQuery: Ka Kb conjugate pair Kw acetate Kb calculation

cards.title: In the reaction $\ce{BF3 + NH3 -> F3B-NH3}$, which reactant acts as the Lewis acid?
cards.body:
$\ce{BF3}$

A **Lewis acid** accepts an electron pair (here into boron's empty $2p$ orbital); $\ce{NH3}$ donates its lone pair as the Lewis base.

Watch out: no $\ce{H+}$ moves, so this isn't a Brønsted-Lowry acid-base reaction (acid = proton donor, base = proton acceptor).
cards.searchQuery: Lewis acid electron pair acceptor BF3 NH3

cards.title: A buffer is $0.20\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{CH3COO-}$ and $0.10\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{CH3COOH}$ ($\mathrm{p}K_a = 4.74$). What is its pH, to two decimal places?
cards.body:
5.04

Henderson-Hasselbalch: $\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a + \log\dfrac{[\ce{A-}]}{[\ce{HA}]} = 4.74 + \log 2.0 = 4.74 + 0.30$.

More base than acid puts the pH **above** the $\mathrm{p}K_a$.

Watch out: flipping the ratio gives 4.44.
cards.searchQuery: Henderson-Hasselbalch buffer pH calculation acetate acetic acid

cards.title: In an acetic acid/acetate buffer, which species reacts with added strong acid, and what does it form?
cards.body:
Acetate: $\ce{CH3COO- + H3O+ -> CH3COOH + H2O}$

Added $\ce{OH-}$ is consumed by the weak acid instead: $\ce{CH3COOH + OH- -> CH3COO- + H2O}$.

Only the ratio $[\ce{A-}]/[\ce{HA}]$ changes a little, so the pH barely moves.

Tip: buffers work best within $\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a \pm 1$.
cards.searchQuery: how a buffer neutralizes added strong acid acetate

cards.title: In a weak acid-strong base titration, what does the pH equal at the half-equivalence point?
cards.body:
$\mathrm{p}K_a$ of the weak acid

Halfway to equivalence, half of the $\ce{HA}$ has become $\ce{A-}$, so $[\ce{HA}] = [\ce{A-}]$ and $\log 1 = 0$ in Henderson-Hasselbalch.

That's how $K_a$ is read from a titration curve.

Watch out: at the equivalence point itself the pH is above 7, because $\ce{A-}$ is basic.
cards.searchQuery: half-equivalence point pH equals pKa weak acid titration

cards.title: For $\ce{PbCl2(s) <=> Pb^2+(aq) + 2Cl-(aq)}$, express $K_{sp}$ in terms of the molar solubility $s$.
cards.body:
$K_{sp} = 4s^3$

Dissolving $s$ mol/L gives $[\ce{Pb^2+}] = s$ and $[\ce{Cl-}] = 2s$, so $K_{sp} = (s)(2s)^2 = 4s^3$.

Watch out: don't forget to **square the $2s$**.
Tip: compare $K_{sp}$ values directly only for salts with the same ion ratio.
cards.searchQuery: Ksp molar solubility PbCl2 4s^3

cards.title: How does dissolving $\ce{NaCl}$ in the water change the molar solubility of $\ce{AgCl}$, and why?
cards.body:
It **decreases** it (the common-ion effect).

Extra $\ce{Cl-}$ pushes $\ce{AgCl(s) <=> Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq)}$ to the left, so less solid dissolves. $K_{sp}$ itself doesn't change.

Once the added chloride dominates, $s \approx K_{sp}/[\ce{Cl-}]$.

Key idea: a shared ion lowers solubility.
cards.searchQuery: common ion effect AgCl solubility NaCl Ksp

cards.title: At dynamic equilibrium, what is equal and what stays constant?
cards.body:
The forward and reverse **rates** are equal, so the concentrations stay constant.

Both reactions are still running; their effects cancel. That is why it is called dynamic, and why the macroscopic properties (color, pressure, pH) stop changing.

Watch out: equal **rates**, not equal concentrations.
cards.searchQuery: dynamic equilibrium forward and reverse rates equal

cards.title: Write the equilibrium constant $K_c$ for $\ce{aA + bB <=> cC + dD}$.
cards.body:
$K_c = \dfrac{[\ce{C}]^c[\ce{D}]^d}{[\ce{A}]^a[\ce{B}]^b}$

**Products over reactants**, each concentration raised to its stoichiometric coefficient, all measured at equilibrium.

Tip: write $K$ from the balanced equation as given. Changing the coefficients changes $K$.
cards.searchQuery: equilibrium constant expression law of mass action products over reactants

cards.title: Write $K_c$ for $\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g)}$.
cards.body:
$K_c = \dfrac{[\ce{NH3}]^2}{[\ce{N2}][\ce{H2}]^3}$

Each coefficient becomes an exponent: 2 for $\ce{NH3}$ in the numerator, 1 and 3 for the reactants below.

Watch out: the **coefficient** is the exponent, not a multiplier.
cards.searchQuery: Kc expression Haber process ammonia synthesis

cards.title: What does $K \gg 1$ tell you about a reaction at equilibrium, and what does $K \ll 1$ tell you?
cards.body:
$K \gg 1$: **products** are favored. $K \ll 1$: **reactants** are favored.

When $K$ is near 1, significant amounts of both are present.

Watch out: $K$ says where equilibrium lies, not how fast it gets there. A reaction with a huge $K$ can still be extremely slow.
cards.searchQuery: meaning of large and small equilibrium constant K products favored

cards.title: A reaction has $K_c = 50$. What is $K_c$ for the reverse reaction, as a decimal?
cards.body:
0.02

Reversing a reaction **inverts** $K$: $K_{\mathrm{rev}} = 1/K_{\mathrm{fwd}} = 1/50$.

Example: a forward $K$ of $10^3$ becomes $10^{-3}$ when the equation is written backward.
cards.searchQuery: equilibrium constant of reverse reaction reciprocal

cards.title: $\ce{A <=> B}$ has $K = 4.0$. What is $K$ for $\ce{2A <=> 2B}$?
cards.body:
16

Multiplying the coefficients by $n$ raises $K$ to the **$n$th power**: $K_{\mathrm{new}} = K^n = 4.0^2$.

Why: each concentration in the expression is raised to its coefficient, so doubling every coefficient squares the whole ratio.
cards.searchQuery: equilibrium constant when equation multiplied by factor K to the n

cards.title: Two reactions with $K_1 = 2.0$ and $K_2 = 5.0$ are added to give an overall reaction. What is $K_{\mathrm{overall}}$?
cards.body:
10

When reactions are added, their equilibrium constants **multiply**: $K = K_1K_2$.

Compare: enthalpies add under Hess's law, but $K$ values multiply because $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$ and the logs add.
cards.searchQuery: equilibrium constant of sum of reactions multiply K1 K2

cards.title: Write $K_a$ for $\ce{HF(aq) + H2O(l) <=> H3O+(aq) + F-(aq)}$.
cards.body:
$K_a = \dfrac{[\ce{H3O+}][\ce{F-}]}{[\ce{HF}]}$

Liquid water is the solvent and is **left out** of the expression, just like a pure liquid.

Tip: the same form works with $[\ce{H+}]$ in place of $[\ce{H3O+}]$.
cards.searchQuery: Ka expression weak acid HF water omitted

cards.title: Does the thermodynamic equilibrium constant $K$ have units?
cards.body:
No: it is dimensionless.

$K$ is defined with activities, which are concentrations divided by the standard state (1 M for solutes, 1 bar for gases). The units cancel.

Many courses still write $K_c$ and $K_p$ without units, or sometimes with them. Follow your instructor on that.

Key idea: $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$ only makes sense because $K$ is unitless.
cards.searchQuery: equilibrium constant dimensionless activities standard state units

cards.title: A mixture of $\ce{N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g)}$ at equilibrium has $[\ce{N2O4}] = 0.040\,\mathrm{M}$ and $[\ce{NO2}] = 0.12\,\mathrm{M}$. What is $K_c$ (number only)?
cards.body:
0.36

$K_c = \dfrac{[\ce{NO2}]^2}{[\ce{N2O4}]} = \dfrac{(0.12)^2}{0.040} = \dfrac{0.0144}{0.040}$.

Watch out: **square** the $\ce{NO2}$ concentration before dividing.
cards.searchQuery: calculate Kc from equilibrium concentrations N2O4 NO2

cards.title: $\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$ has $K_c = 50$. A mixture has $[\ce{H2}] = [\ce{I2}] = 0.50\,\mathrm{M}$ and $[\ce{HI}] = 1.0\,\mathrm{M}$. What is $Q$?
cards.body:
4

$Q = \dfrac{[\ce{HI}]^2}{[\ce{H2}][\ce{I2}]} = \dfrac{(1.0)^2}{(0.50)(0.50)} = 4.0$.

Since $Q < K$ ($4 < 50$), the reaction proceeds **forward**, making more $\ce{HI}$.
cards.searchQuery: reaction quotient Q calculation H2 I2 HI compare to K

cards.title: What does ICE stand for in an equilibrium calculation, and which row goes into the $K$ expression?
cards.body:
**I**nitial, **C**hange, **E**quilibrium. The **E row** goes into $K$.

The Change row follows the stoichiometry: for $\ce{A <=> 2B}$ it is $-x$ and $+2x$.

Watch out: don't substitute the initial concentrations into $K$; that gives $Q$.
cards.searchQuery: ICE table initial change equilibrium method

cards.title: For $\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$, suppose $K_c = 64$ (hypothetical). Starting with $1.0\,\mathrm{M}$ each of $\ce{H2}$ and $\ce{I2}$ and no HI, what is $[\ce{HI}]$ at equilibrium, in M?
cards.body:
1.6

Let $x$ be the amount of $\ce{H2}$ used up: $K_c = \dfrac{(2x)^2}{(1.0 - x)^2} = 64$.

The right side is a perfect square, so take the square root: $\dfrac{2x}{1.0 - x} = 8$, giving $x = 0.80$ and $[\ce{HI}] = 2x = 1.6\,\mathrm{M}$.

Tip: look for perfect squares before reaching for the quadratic formula.
cards.searchQuery: ICE table equilibrium concentration calculation perfect square H2 I2 HI

cards.title: In an ICE problem, when may you drop $x$ from an expression like $[\ce{A}]_0 - x$?
cards.body:
When $K$ is small compared with $[\ce{A}]_0$, so $x$ is under about 5% of $[\ce{A}]_0$.

A rough guide is $[\ce{A}]_0/K > 400$. Always **check** afterward that $x/[\ce{A}]_0 < 5\%$; if not, solve the quadratic.

Watch out: the shortcut fails for dilute solutions of fairly strong weak acids.
cards.searchQuery: 5 percent rule small x approximation equilibrium ICE

cards.title: Write $K_p$ for $\ce{N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g)}$.
cards.body:
$K_p = \dfrac{P_{\ce{NO2}}^2}{P_{\ce{N2O4}}}$

For gases, use **partial pressures** (in atm or bar) in place of concentrations.

Tip: partial pressure is mole fraction times total pressure: $P_i = X_iP_{\mathrm{total}}$.
cards.searchQuery: Kp expression partial pressures N2O4 NO2

cards.title: $\ce{N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g)}$ has $K_c = 0.0100$ at $300\,\mathrm{K}$. What is $K_p$, to three significant figures? ($R = 0.08206\,\mathrm{L\,atm/(mol\,K)}$)
cards.body:
0.246

$\Delta n = 2 - 1 = +1$, so $K_p = K_c(RT)^1 = 0.0100 \times (0.08206 \times 300) = 0.0100 \times 24.6$.

Watch out: use $R$ in L atm units and $T$ in kelvin, matching the pressure unit of $K_p$.
cards.searchQuery: convert Kc to Kp calculation delta n RT N2O4

cards.title: For $\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g)}$ at $500\,\mathrm{K}$, is $K_p$ larger or smaller than $K_c$?
cards.body:
Smaller

$\Delta n = 2 - 4 = -2$, so $K_p = K_c(RT)^{-2}$. With $RT = 0.08206 \times 500 \approx 41$, $K_p \approx K_c/1700$.

Tip: when $\Delta n < 0$ and $RT > 1$, $K_p < K_c$; when $\Delta n > 0$, $K_p > K_c$.
cards.searchQuery: Kp smaller than Kc negative delta n Haber

cards.title: Can the same equilibrium mixture be reached starting from pure products instead of pure reactants?
cards.body:
Yes, at the same temperature (and total amounts of each element).

The equilibrium composition depends on $K$ and the **total** amounts of atoms, not on which side you start from.

Example: $\ce{H2 + I2 <=> 2HI}$ gives the same equilibrium from $\ce{H2}$ and $\ce{I2}$ as from the right amount of $\ce{HI}$ alone.
cards.searchQuery: equilibrium reached from either direction same composition

cards.title: $\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g)}$ is at equilibrium. More $\ce{N2}$ is added at constant volume. Which way does it shift?
cards.body:
right

Adding a reactant makes $Q < K$, so the reaction runs **forward** to consume part of the added $\ce{N2}$.

$K$ is unchanged, and $[\ce{NH3}]$ rises.

Watch out: the new $[\ce{N2}]$ is still higher than before; the system only partly offsets the change.
cards.searchQuery: Le Chatelier add reactant shift right Haber process

cards.title: Why is $\ce{NH3}$ condensed to a liquid and removed in the Haber process?
cards.body:
Removing the product keeps $Q < K$, so the reaction keeps shifting **forward**.

Ammonia liquefies far more easily than $\ce{N2}$ or $\ce{H2}$. The unreacted gases are recycled back to the reactor.

Key idea: removing a product pulls the equilibrium toward products.
cards.searchQuery: Haber process ammonia removal condensing shift equilibrium

cards.title: $\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g)}$ has $\Delta H = -92\,\mathrm{kJ}$. Which way does the equilibrium shift when the temperature is raised?
cards.body:
left

For an exothermic reaction, heat acts like a **product**. Adding heat shifts the equilibrium toward the reactants, and $K$ decreases.

Why: the system absorbs the added heat by running the endothermic (reverse) direction.

Tip: write "+ heat" on the product side of an exothermic equation, then treat it like any other species.
cards.searchQuery: Le Chatelier temperature increase exothermic reaction shifts left

cards.title: $\ce{N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g)}$ is endothermic ($\Delta H = +57\,\mathrm{kJ}$). What happens to the brown color and to $K$ when the mixture is heated?
cards.body:
It darkens, and $K$ increases.

Heating shifts an endothermic equilibrium **to the right**, making more brown $\ce{NO2}$ (colorless $\ce{N2O4}$ is consumed).

Key idea: temperature is the only change that alters $K$ itself.
cards.searchQuery: N2O4 NO2 equilibrium heating color change endothermic

cards.title: Argon is added at constant total pressure to an equilibrium mixture of $\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g)}$. Which way does it shift?
cards.body:
left

At constant pressure the volume grows, so the partial pressures of the reacting gases all fall.

The system opposes this by shifting toward the side with **more moles of gas**, here the reactant side (4 mol vs 2 mol).

Watch out: the same argon added at constant **volume** causes no shift.
cards.searchQuery: inert gas added constant pressure equilibrium shift more moles of gas

cards.title: What effect does adding a catalyst have on the position of an equilibrium?
cards.body:
none

A catalyst lowers the barrier for the forward and reverse reactions **equally**, so $K$ and the equilibrium composition are unchanged.

It only lets the system reach equilibrium sooner.
cards.searchQuery: catalyst effect on equilibrium position no change

cards.title: $\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$ is at equilibrium. Which way does it shift when the volume is halved?
cards.body:
none

There are 2 mol of gas on each side, so compression raises the rates of both directions equally and $Q$ stays equal to $K$.

All concentrations double, but their ratio is unchanged.

Tip: check $\Delta n_{\mathrm{gas}}$ first. If it is zero, pressure and volume changes do nothing.
cards.searchQuery: equal moles of gas pressure change no shift H2 I2 HI

cards.title: $\ce{CaCO3(s) <=> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$ is at equilibrium. What happens to the amount of $\ce{CO2}$ when more $\ce{CaO(s)}$ is added?
cards.body:
Nothing: there is no shift.

A pure solid does not appear in $K$, so adding more of it leaves $Q = K$.

Watch out: changing the **volume** would shift the equilibrium, because $\ce{CO2(g)}$ is a gas.
cards.searchQuery: adding pure solid to equilibrium no shift Le Chatelier CaCO3

cards.title: $\ce{Fe^3+(aq) + SCN-(aq) <=> FeSCN^2+(aq)}$ (red). Which way does it shift, and what happens to the color, when water is added?
cards.body:
Left; the red color fades.

Diluting lowers every concentration, and the system partly offsets this by favoring the side with **more dissolved particles**: 2 on the left, 1 on the right.

Example: adding more $\ce{Fe^3+}$ instead shifts the equilibrium right and the solution turns a deeper red.
cards.searchQuery: iron thiocyanate equilibrium dilution shift left color

cards.title: Write the van't Hoff equation that gives $K_2$ at $T_2$ from $K_1$ at $T_1$.
cards.body:
$\ln\dfrac{K_2}{K_1} = -\dfrac{\Delta H^\circ}{R}\left(\dfrac{1}{T_2} - \dfrac{1}{T_1}\right)$

If $\Delta H^\circ > 0$ and $T_2 > T_1$, the right side is positive, so $K$ rises. If $\Delta H^\circ < 0$, $K$ falls.

Watch out: use $R = 8.314\,\mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}$ with $\Delta H^\circ$ in joules, and $T$ in kelvin.
cards.searchQuery: van't Hoff equation K temperature dependence enthalpy

cards.title: Give the Brønsted-Lowry definitions of an acid and a base.
cards.body:
An **acid** donates a proton ($\ce{H+}$); a **base** accepts a proton.

In $\ce{HCl + H2O -> Cl- + H3O+}$, $\ce{HCl}$ is the acid and $\ce{H2O}$ is the base.

Key idea: acid-base reactions are proton transfers, and every acid has a conjugate base that is one proton lighter.
cards.searchQuery: Bronsted-Lowry acid proton donor base proton acceptor definition

cards.title: What is the conjugate base of $\ce{H2PO4-}$?
cards.body:
$\ce{HPO4^2-}$

A conjugate base is the acid minus one $\ce{H+}$: remove a proton and the charge drops by 1.

Compare: $\ce{H2PO4-}$ is also the conjugate base of $\ce{H3PO4}$, so it is amphiprotic.
cards.searchQuery: conjugate base of H2PO4- hydrogen phosphate

cards.title: What is the conjugate acid of $\ce{NH3}$?
cards.body:
$\ce{NH4+}$

A conjugate acid is the base **plus** one $\ce{H+}$: $\ce{NH3 + H+ -> NH4+}$.

The conjugate acid of a weak base is a weak acid, which is why $\ce{NH4Cl}$ solutions are slightly acidic.
cards.searchQuery: conjugate acid of ammonia ammonium ion

cards.title: What does amphiprotic mean? Use the bicarbonate ion $\ce{HCO3-}$ as the example.
cards.body:
An amphiprotic species can **both donate and accept** a proton.

$\ce{HCO3-}$ donates: $\ce{HCO3- -> CO3^2- + H+}$. It accepts: $\ce{HCO3- + H+ -> H2CO3}$.

Example: water is also amphiprotic ($\ce{H3O+}$ and $\ce{OH-}$ are its conjugates).
cards.searchQuery: amphiprotic species donate and accept proton bicarbonate

cards.title: Define pH. By what factor does $[\ce{H3O+}]$ change when the pH changes by 1 unit?
cards.body:
$\mathrm{pH} = -\log[\ce{H3O+}]$; a change of 1 unit is a factor of **10**.

So a pH 3 solution has 100 times the $[\ce{H3O+}]$ of a pH 5 solution.

Watch out: lower pH means **more** acidic.
cards.searchQuery: definition of pH negative log hydronium concentration

cards.title: What is the pH of $0.0025\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{HCl}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, to two decimal places?
cards.body:
2.60

$\ce{HCl}$ is a strong acid, so $[\ce{H3O+}] = 0.0025\,\mathrm{M}$ and $\mathrm{pH} = -\log(2.5 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.60$.

Tip: $-\log(2.5 \times 10^{-3}) = 3 - \log 2.5 = 3 - 0.40$.
cards.searchQuery: pH of strong acid HCl calculation concentration

cards.title: What is the pH of $0.010\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{Ba(OH)2}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, to two decimal places?
cards.body:
12.30

Each formula unit releases two hydroxides, so $[\ce{OH-}] = 2(0.010) = 0.020\,\mathrm{M}$.

Then $\mathrm{pOH} = -\log(0.020) = 1.70$ and $\mathrm{pH} = 14.00 - 1.70$.

Watch out: forgetting the factor of 2 gives 12.00.
cards.searchQuery: pH of barium hydroxide solution two hydroxides per formula unit

cards.title: What is the pH of $1.0 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{HCl}$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, to two decimal places?
cards.body:
6.98

The acid's $10^{-8}\,\mathrm{M}$ is comparable to water's own $10^{-7}\,\mathrm{M}$, so water's autoionization **can't be ignored**.

Solving $[\ce{H3O+}] = 10^{-8} + x$ with $x(x + 10^{-8}) = 10^{-14}$ gives $[\ce{H3O+}] \approx 1.05 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{M}$.

Watch out: the naive answer 8.00 would be a basic pH for an acid.
cards.searchQuery: pH of very dilute strong acid 1e-8 M HCl water autoionization

cards.title: A solution has pH $3.20$. What is $[\ce{H3O+}]$ in M, to two significant figures?
cards.body:
$6.3 \times 10^{-4}$

$[\ce{H3O+}] = 10^{-\mathrm{pH}} = 10^{-3.20}$. Since $10^{-0.20} \approx 0.63$, this is $0.63 \times 10^{-3}$.

Tip: pH 3.20 lies between 3 and 4, so the answer must lie between $10^{-3}$ and $10^{-4}$, closer to $10^{-3}$.
cards.searchQuery: hydronium concentration from pH antilog calculation

cards.title: A weak acid has $K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$. What is its $\mathrm{p}K_a$, to two decimal places?
cards.body:
4.74

$\mathrm{p}K_a = -\log K_a = -\log(1.8 \times 10^{-5}) = 5 - 0.255 = 4.74$.

Tip: for $K_a = a \times 10^{-n}$, the $\mathrm{p}K_a$ lies between $n - 1$ and $n$.
cards.searchQuery: calculate pKa from Ka acetic acid 4.74

cards.title: Which is the stronger acid: $\ce{HF}$ ($\mathrm{p}K_a \approx 3.2$) or acetic acid ($\mathrm{p}K_a = 4.74$)?
cards.body:
$\ce{HF}$

A **lower** $\mathrm{p}K_a$ means a larger $K_a$ and a stronger acid. The $1.5$-unit gap makes $\ce{HF}$ roughly 30 times more acidic.

Watch out: a strong-acid label is about complete ionization; both of these are weak acids.
cards.searchQuery: compare acid strength using pKa lower pKa stronger acid

cards.title: Which hydroxides are the common strong bases?
cards.body:
Group 1 hydroxides ($\ce{LiOH}$, $\ce{NaOH}$, $\ce{KOH}$, ...) and the heavier group 2 hydroxides $\ce{Ca(OH)2}$, $\ce{Sr(OH)2}$, $\ce{Ba(OH)2}$.

They dissociate completely in water. $\ce{Ca(OH)2}$ is not very soluble, but what dissolves is fully dissociated.

Watch out: $\ce{NH3}$ is a **weak** base; it only partly reacts with water.
cards.searchQuery: common strong bases list group 1 hydroxides Ba(OH)2 Ca(OH)2

cards.title: At $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, what is $\mathrm{p}K_w$ (that is, $\mathrm{pH} + \mathrm{pOH}$)?
cards.body:
14

Taking $-\log$ of $K_w = [\ce{H3O+}][\ce{OH-}] = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}$ gives $\mathrm{pH} + \mathrm{pOH} = 14.00$.

Watch out: this sum equals 14 only near $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, because $K_w$ changes with temperature.
cards.searchQuery: pKw 14 pH plus pOH at 25 C

cards.title: What is the pH of $0.10\,\mathrm{M}$ acetic acid ($K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$), to two decimal places?
cards.body:
2.87

$K_a = \dfrac{x^2}{0.10 - x} \approx \dfrac{x^2}{0.10}$, so $x = \sqrt{1.8 \times 10^{-6}} = 1.3 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{M} = [\ce{H3O+}]$.

Then $\mathrm{pH} = -\log(1.34 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.87$. The approximation is fine because $x$ is only 1.3% of 0.10.

Watch out: a strong acid at this concentration would give pH 1.00.
cards.searchQuery: pH of weak acid acetic acid 0.10 M Ka calculation

cards.title: What is the percent ionization of $0.10\,\mathrm{M}$ acetic acid ($K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$)? Give the percentage to two significant figures, number only.
cards.body:
1.3

$x = [\ce{H3O+}] = 1.34 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{M}$, so $\%\ \text{ionization} = \dfrac{x}{[\ce{HA}]_0} \times 100 = \dfrac{1.34 \times 10^{-3}}{0.10} \times 100$.

Only about 1 molecule in 75 is ionized: a **weak** acid stays mostly intact.
cards.searchQuery: percent ionization weak acid acetic acid calculation

cards.title: How does the percent ionization of a weak acid change when its solution is diluted?
cards.body:
It **increases**.

Dilution shifts $\ce{HA + H2O <=> H3O+ + A-}$ toward more dissolved particles, so a larger fraction ionizes, even though $[\ce{H3O+}]$ itself falls.

Example: acetic acid is about 1.3% ionized at $0.10\,\mathrm{M}$ and about 4.2% at $0.010\,\mathrm{M}$.
cards.searchQuery: weak acid dilution percent ionization increases Ostwald

cards.title: What is the pH of $0.20\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{NH3}$ ($K_b = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$) at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, to two decimal places?
cards.body:
11.28

$\ce{NH3 + H2O <=> NH4+ + OH-}$: $x = [\ce{OH-}] = \sqrt{(1.8 \times 10^{-5})(0.20)} = 1.9 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{M}$.

Then $\mathrm{pOH} = 2.72$ and $\mathrm{pH} = 14.00 - 2.72 = 11.28$.

Watch out: the unknown $x$ is $[\ce{OH-}]$ here, so you get **pOH** first.
cards.searchQuery: pH of weak base ammonia Kb calculation 0.20 M

cards.title: Is a solution of $\ce{NH4Cl}$ acidic, basic or neutral?
cards.body:
acidic

$\ce{NH4+}$ is the conjugate acid of the weak base $\ce{NH3}$, so it donates protons to water: $\ce{NH4+ + H2O <=> NH3 + H3O+}$.

$\ce{Cl-}$ is the conjugate base of a strong acid and does nothing.

Tip: a salt's pH comes from the ions of **weak** acids or bases.
cards.searchQuery: ammonium chloride solution acidic hydrolysis salt

cards.title: Is a solution of sodium acetate, $\ce{CH3COONa}$, acidic, basic or neutral?
cards.body:
basic

Acetate is the conjugate base of a weak acid, so it takes protons from water: $\ce{CH3COO- + H2O <=> CH3COOH + OH-}$.

$\ce{Na+}$ is a spectator.
cards.searchQuery: sodium acetate solution basic hydrolysis conjugate base

cards.title: Which of these salts gives a neutral aqueous solution: $\ce{NH4Cl}$, $\ce{NaF}$, $\ce{KNO3}$ or $\ce{Na2CO3}$?
cards.body:
$\ce{KNO3}$

Both $\ce{K+}$ (from a strong base) and $\ce{NO3-}$ (from a strong acid) are too weak as acid and base to react with water.

The others contain an ion of a weak acid or weak base: $\ce{NH4+}$ (acidic), $\ce{F-}$ and $\ce{CO3^2-}$ (basic).
cards.searchQuery: neutral salt strong acid strong base ions KNO3 hydrolysis

cards.title: What is the pH of $0.10\,\mathrm{M}$ sodium acetate? ($K_a$ of acetic acid $= 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$.) Two decimal places.
cards.body:
8.87

First $K_b = K_w/K_a = 5.6 \times 10^{-10}$. Then $[\ce{OH-}] = \sqrt{(5.6 \times 10^{-10})(0.10)} = 7.5 \times 10^{-6}\,\mathrm{M}$.

$\mathrm{pOH} = 5.13$, so $\mathrm{pH} = 14.00 - 5.13 = 8.87$.

Watch out: use $K_b$ of the **acetate**, not the $K_a$ of the acid.
cards.searchQuery: pH of sodium acetate solution Kb from Ka calculation

cards.title: Write the reaction that makes aqueous $\ce{NaF}$ slightly basic.
cards.body:
$\ce{F- + H2O <=> HF + OH-}$

Fluoride is the conjugate base of the weak acid $\ce{HF}$, so it grabs a proton from water and releases $\ce{OH-}$.

For this reaction $K_b = K_w/K_a(\ce{HF})$.

Watch out: $\ce{Na+}$ does not appear; it is a spectator.
cards.searchQuery: fluoride ion hydrolysis equation NaF basic solution

cards.title: $25.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $0.100\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{HCl}$ is mixed with $15.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $0.100\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{NaOH}$. What is the pH, to two decimal places?
cards.body:
1.60

$2.50\,\mathrm{mmol}$ of $\ce{H3O+}$ minus $1.50\,\mathrm{mmol}$ of $\ce{OH-}$ leaves $1.00\,\mathrm{mmol}$ of acid in $40.0\,\mathrm{mL}$.

$[\ce{H3O+}] = 0.0250\,\mathrm{M}$, so $\mathrm{pH} = 1.60$.

Watch out: divide by the **total** volume, 40.0 mL, not 25.0 mL.
cards.searchQuery: pH after mixing strong acid and strong base excess calculation

cards.title: What is the difference between a strong acid and a concentrated acid?
cards.body:
**Strength** is how completely the acid ionizes; **concentration** is how much acid is dissolved.

A dilute $\ce{HCl}$ solution is a strong acid at low concentration. Concentrated acetic acid is a weak acid at high concentration.

Watch out: don't judge the pH from the label alone; compute it from $K_a$ and the concentration.
cards.searchQuery: strong acid versus concentrated acid difference ionization

cards.title: Which is the stronger acid, $\ce{HCl}$ or $\ce{HI}$, and what decides the trend down a group?
cards.body:
$\ce{HI}$

Down a group the $\ce{H-X}$ bond gets **longer and weaker**, so it breaks more easily; this outweighs the fall in electronegativity.

Across a period the opposite factor wins: $\ce{CH4} < \ce{NH3} < \ce{H2O} < \ce{HF}$ in acidity, because electronegativity stabilizes the anion.
cards.searchQuery: binary acid strength trend HI HCl bond strength periodic

cards.title: Rank $\ce{HClO}$, $\ce{HClO2}$, $\ce{HClO3}$ and $\ce{HClO4}$ by acid strength.
cards.body:
$\ce{HClO} < \ce{HClO2} < \ce{HClO3} < \ce{HClO4}$

More oxygen atoms on the central atom pull electron density away from the $\ce{O-H}$ bond and spread the negative charge of the anion over more oxygens.

Key idea: for oxyacids with the same central atom, more $\ce{O}$ means a stronger acid.
cards.searchQuery: oxyacid strength trend chlorine oxoacids HClO4 strongest

cards.title: Why is $K_{a2}$ much smaller than $K_{a1}$ for a polyprotic acid such as $\ce{H3PO4}$?
cards.body:
Removing a proton from a **negatively charged** ion is harder than from a neutral molecule.

So $K_{a1} \gg K_{a2} \gg K_{a3}$, typically by several orders of magnitude per step.

Tip: for most polyprotic acids, the pH comes almost entirely from the first ionization.
cards.searchQuery: polyprotic acid successive Ka values decrease H3PO4

cards.title: What is the strongest acid that can exist in water, and the strongest base?
cards.body:
$\ce{H3O+}$ and $\ce{OH-}$

Any stronger acid reacts completely with water to form $\ce{H3O+}$, and any stronger base forms $\ce{OH-}$. This is the **leveling effect**.

That's why $\ce{HCl}$ and $\ce{HNO3}$ look equally strong in water.
cards.searchQuery: leveling effect water strongest acid H3O+ strongest base OH-

cards.title: Write the net ionic equation for a strong acid reacting with a strong base in water.
cards.body:
$\ce{H3O+ + OH- -> 2H2O}$

The other ions (for example $\ce{Na+}$ and $\ce{Cl-}$ from $\ce{HCl + NaOH}$) are spectators.

It is also commonly written $\ce{H+ + OH- -> H2O}$.
cards.searchQuery: net ionic equation strong acid strong base neutralization

cards.title: In $\ce{Ag+ + 2NH3 -> [Ag(NH3)2]+}$, which reactant is the Lewis base?
cards.body:
$\ce{NH3}$

Ammonia donates a lone pair on nitrogen to $\ce{Ag+}$, which accepts the pairs as the Lewis acid.

Metal-ligand complex formation is a Lewis acid-base reaction: the metal ion is the acid and each ligand is a base.
cards.searchQuery: Lewis base electron pair donor ammonia silver complex ion

cards.title: Write $K_b$ for $\ce{NH3(aq) + H2O(l) <=> NH4+(aq) + OH-(aq)}$.
cards.body:
$K_b = \dfrac{[\ce{NH4+}][\ce{OH-}]}{[\ce{NH3}]}$

As with $K_a$, liquid water is the solvent and is left out.

Key idea: $K_b$ describes a base reacting with water to give its conjugate acid and $\ce{OH-}$.
cards.searchQuery: Kb expression ammonia weak base equilibrium

cards.title: What two components make up a buffer?
cards.body:
A weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid), both present in appreciable amounts.

Examples: $\ce{CH3COOH}$/$\ce{CH3COO-}$ and $\ce{NH4+}$/$\ce{NH3}$.

Watch out: a strong acid and its conjugate base (such as $\ce{HCl}$/$\ce{Cl-}$) is **not** a buffer.
cards.searchQuery: buffer solution composition weak acid conjugate base

cards.title: A $1.00\,\mathrm{L}$ buffer has $0.10\,\mathrm{mol}$ each of $\ce{CH3COOH}$ and $\ce{CH3COO-}$ ($\mathrm{p}K_a = 4.74$). What is the pH after adding $0.010\,\mathrm{mol}$ $\ce{HCl}$?
cards.body:
4.65

The added $\ce{H3O+}$ converts acetate to acetic acid: $\ce{CH3COO-}$ drops to $0.090$ and $\ce{CH3COOH}$ rises to $0.110$.

$\mathrm{pH} = 4.74 + \log\dfrac{0.090}{0.110} = 4.74 - 0.09 = 4.65$.

Tip: do the stoichiometry first (full reaction), then Henderson-Hasselbalch. The volume cancels in the ratio.
cards.searchQuery: buffer pH after adding strong acid stoichiometry Henderson-Hasselbalch

cards.title: A buffer's pH is exactly 1 unit above the $\mathrm{p}K_a$ of its acid. What is the ratio $[\ce{A-}]/[\ce{HA}]$?
cards.body:
10

From $\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a + \log([\ce{A-}]/[\ce{HA}])$, a difference of $+1$ means $\log(\text{ratio}) = 1$.

So the ratio is 10:1, and a pH one unit **below** the $\mathrm{p}K_a$ gives 1:10.
cards.searchQuery: buffer ratio base to acid pH one unit above pKa

cards.title: What two things make a buffer resist added acid or base well?
cards.body:
**High concentrations** of both components, and a **ratio near 1:1**, so $\mathrm{pH} \approx \mathrm{p}K_a$.

The buffer is overwhelmed once one component is nearly used up.

Tip: choose the acid whose $\mathrm{p}K_a$ is closest to the target pH.
cards.searchQuery: buffer capacity concentration ratio near one pKa

cards.title: Which pair makes the best buffer near pH 9.2: acetic acid/acetate ($\mathrm{p}K_a$ 4.74), $\ce{H2CO3}$/$\ce{HCO3-}$ (6.35), $\ce{NH4+}$/$\ce{NH3}$ (9.25) or $\ce{HF}$/$\ce{F-}$ (3.17)?
cards.body:
$\ce{NH4+}$/$\ce{NH3}$

Its $\mathrm{p}K_a$ of 9.25 is closest to the target pH, so $[\ce{NH3}] \approx [\ce{NH4+}]$.

Key idea: pick a pair with $\mathrm{p}K_a$ within $\pm 1$ of the desired pH.
cards.searchQuery: choose buffer pair pKa closest to target pH ammonium ammonia

cards.title: A buffer is $0.30\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{NH3}$ and $0.20\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{NH4Cl}$. With $\mathrm{p}K_a(\ce{NH4+}) = 9.25$, what is the pH, to two decimals?
cards.body:
9.43

$\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a + \log\dfrac{[\ce{NH3}]}{[\ce{NH4+}]} = 9.25 + \log 1.5 = 9.25 + 0.18$.

Watch out: the **base** is $\ce{NH3}$, so it goes in the numerator with the $\mathrm{p}K_a$ of the conjugate acid $\ce{NH4+}$.
cards.searchQuery: ammonia ammonium buffer pH Henderson-Hasselbalch calculation

cards.title: A buffer is diluted tenfold with pure water. What happens to its pH and to its capacity?
cards.body:
The pH stays nearly the same; the capacity drops.

The ratio $[\ce{A-}]/[\ce{HA}]$ is unchanged, so Henderson-Hasselbalch gives the same pH. But there is far less buffering material to absorb added acid or base.

Watch out: at extreme dilution the buffer fails and water's own ions matter.
cards.searchQuery: dilute buffer pH unchanged capacity decreases

cards.title: $0.20\,\mathrm{mol}$ of a weak acid $\ce{HA}$ is mixed with $0.10\,\mathrm{mol}$ of $\ce{NaOH}$. What is the pH in terms of $\mathrm{p}K_a$?
cards.body:
$\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a$

The hydroxide converts half of the $\ce{HA}$ to $\ce{A-}$, leaving $0.10\,\mathrm{mol}$ of each, a 1:1 buffer.

This is the same situation as the half-equivalence point of a titration.

Tip: weak acid plus **less than the equivalent** strong base makes a buffer.
cards.searchQuery: make buffer by partial neutralization weak acid with NaOH half

cards.title: How many mL of $0.125\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{NaOH}$ neutralize $25.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $0.100\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{HCl}$? Give the number only.
cards.body:
20.0

Moles of acid: $0.0250\,\mathrm{L} \times 0.100\,\mathrm{M} = 2.50\,\mathrm{mmol}$.

The acid and base react 1:1, so the volume is $2.50\,\mathrm{mmol} \div 0.125\,\mathrm{M} = 20.0\,\mathrm{mL}$.

Tip: $M_aV_a = M_bV_b$ works only for 1:1 stoichiometry.
cards.searchQuery: titration calculation volume of NaOH to neutralize HCl

cards.title: What is the pH at the equivalence point of a strong acid-strong base titration at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$?
cards.body:
7

The solution holds only a salt of a strong acid and a strong base (for example $\ce{NaCl}$), whose ions don't react with water.

Watch out: only for strong-strong titrations; weak acids and bases give an equivalence-point pH above or below 7.
cards.searchQuery: equivalence point pH strong acid strong base titration 7

cards.title: Is the pH at the equivalence point of acetic acid titrated with $\ce{NaOH}$ below, at or above 7?
cards.body:
Above 7

At equivalence all the acetic acid has become acetate, a weak base: $\ce{CH3COO- + H2O <=> CH3COOH + OH-}$.

The pH is typically about 8.5-9 for a 0.1 M solution.

Key idea: the equivalence-point pH is the pH of the salt formed.
cards.searchQuery: weak acid strong base titration equivalence point pH above 7

cards.title: Is the pH at the equivalence point of $\ce{NH3}$ titrated with $\ce{HCl}$ below, at or above 7?
cards.body:
Below 7

At equivalence the solution contains $\ce{NH4+}$, a weak acid: $\ce{NH4+ + H2O <=> NH3 + H3O+}$.

Key idea: look at the conjugate species left at equivalence.
cards.searchQuery: weak base strong acid titration equivalence point pH below 7

cards.title: Which indicator suits titrating acetic acid with $\ce{NaOH}$: methyl orange (range 3.1-4.4) or phenolphthalein (8.2-10.0)?
cards.body:
Phenolphthalein

Its color change falls on the steep part of the curve, near the equivalence-point pH (above 7).

Methyl orange changes color long before equivalence and would give a wrong end point.

Tip: the indicator's range should include the equivalence-point pH.
cards.searchQuery: indicator choice weak acid strong base titration phenolphthalein

cards.title: Write $K_{sp}$ for $\ce{Ca3(PO4)2(s) <=> 3Ca^2+(aq) + 2PO4^3-(aq)}$.
cards.body:
$K_{sp} = [\ce{Ca^2+}]^3[\ce{PO4^3-}]^2$

The solid is left out. Each ion concentration is raised to its coefficient.

Watch out: don't multiply the concentrations by the coefficients; the coefficients are exponents.
cards.searchQuery: Ksp expression calcium phosphate Ca3(PO4)2

cards.title: $K_{sp}(\ce{AgCl}) = 1.8 \times 10^{-10}$. What is its molar solubility in pure water, in M, to two significant figures?
cards.body:
$1.3 \times 10^{-5}$

For a 1:1 salt, $[\ce{Ag+}] = [\ce{Cl-}] = s$, so $K_{sp} = s^2$ and $s = \sqrt{1.8 \times 10^{-10}}$.

Tip: for a 1:1 salt, $s = \sqrt{K_{sp}}$.
cards.searchQuery: molar solubility of AgCl from Ksp calculation

cards.title: A salt $\ce{MX2}$ has $K_{sp} = 4.0 \times 10^{-12}$. What is its molar solubility $s$ in M?
cards.searchQuery: molar solubility from Ksp for MX2 salt cube root

cards.title: A salt $\ce{MX2}$ has molar solubility $2.0 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{M}$. What is $K_{sp}$, to two significant figures?
cards.body:
$3.2 \times 10^{-11}$

$[\ce{M^2+}] = s$ and $[\ce{X-}] = 2s$, so $K_{sp} = 4s^3 = 4(2.0 \times 10^{-4})^3 = 4(8.0 \times 10^{-12})$.

Watch out: cube $s$ first, then multiply by 4.
cards.searchQuery: calculate Ksp from molar solubility MX2 4s^3

cards.title: A saturated $\ce{BaSO4}$ solution contains $2.33 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{g/L}$ (molar mass $233\,\mathrm{g/mol}$). What is $K_{sp}$?
cards.body:
$1.0 \times 10^{-10}$

Convert first: $s = 2.33 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{g/L} \div 233\,\mathrm{g/mol} = 1.00 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{M}$.

$\ce{BaSO4}$ is 1:1, so $K_{sp} = s^2 = 1.0 \times 10^{-10}$.

Watch out: convert grams per liter to **moles** per liter before using $K_{sp}$.
cards.searchQuery: Ksp from solubility in grams per liter barium sulfate

cards.title: What is the molar solubility of $\ce{AgCl}$ ($K_{sp} = 1.8 \times 10^{-10}$) in $0.10\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{NaCl}$, in M?
cards.body:
$1.8 \times 10^{-9}$

The chloride is essentially all from $\ce{NaCl}$, so $[\ce{Cl-}] \approx 0.10\,\mathrm{M}$ and $s = [\ce{Ag+}] = K_{sp}/0.10$.

That is about 7000 times less soluble than in pure water ($1.3 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{M}$).
cards.searchQuery: AgCl solubility in NaCl solution common ion calculation

cards.title: Equal volumes of $1.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{AgNO3}$ and $1.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{NaCl}$ are mixed. Does $\ce{AgCl}$ ($K_{sp} = 1.8 \times 10^{-10}$) precipitate?
cards.body:
yes

Mixing equal volumes halves each concentration to $5.0 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{M}$, so $Q_{sp} = (5.0 \times 10^{-4})^2 = 2.5 \times 10^{-7}$.

Since $Q_{sp} > K_{sp}$ (by a factor of over 1000), solid forms.

Watch out: use the concentrations **after mixing**.
cards.searchQuery: will precipitate form mixing solutions Qsp compared to Ksp

cards.title: How do you use $Q_{sp}$ and $K_{sp}$ to predict whether a precipitate forms?
cards.body:
$Q_{sp} > K_{sp}$: precipitate forms. $Q_{sp} = K_{sp}$: saturated. $Q_{sp} < K_{sp}$: no precipitate.

$Q_{sp}$ is the ion product with the **current** concentrations, written like $K_{sp}$.

Key idea: same logic as $Q$ vs $K$ for any equilibrium.
cards.searchQuery: Qsp versus Ksp precipitation prediction saturated unsaturated

cards.title: Why does $\ce{Mg(OH)2}$ dissolve more in acidic solution than in pure water?
cards.body:
Acid removes $\ce{OH-}$: $\ce{OH- + H3O+ -> 2H2O}$.

That lowers $[\ce{OH-}]$, so $\ce{Mg(OH)2(s) <=> Mg^2+ + 2OH-}$ shifts **right** to replace it.

Tip: salts of weak-acid anions ($\ce{OH-}$, $\ce{CO3^2-}$, $\ce{F-}$) are more soluble in acid; salts of strong-acid anions ($\ce{Cl-}$) are not.
cards.searchQuery: solubility of hydroxide salts increases in acid pH effect Mg(OH)2

cards.title: $K_{sp}$: $\ce{AgCl}$ $1.8 \times 10^{-10}$; $\ce{Ag2CrO4}$ $1.1 \times 10^{-12}$. Which has the higher molar solubility?
cards.body:
$\ce{Ag2CrO4}$

$\ce{AgCl}$: $s = \sqrt{1.8 \times 10^{-10}} = 1.3 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{M}$.

$\ce{Ag2CrO4}$: $K_{sp} = 4s^3$, so $s = (2.75 \times 10^{-13})^{1/3} = 6.5 \times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{M}$.

Watch out: only compare $K_{sp}$ directly when the formulas have the same ion ratio.
cards.searchQuery: compare solubility from Ksp different stoichiometry Ag2CrO4 AgCl

cards.title: Why does $\ce{AgCl}$ dissolve in aqueous ammonia although it is insoluble in water?
cards.body:
$\ce{Ag+}$ is tied up as the complex ion $\ce{[Ag(NH3)2]+}$.

$\ce{Ag+ + 2NH3 <=> [Ag(NH3)2]+}$ lowers $[\ce{Ag+}]$, so $\ce{AgCl(s) <=> Ag+ + Cl-}$ shifts right.

Key idea: complex formation increases the solubility of many salts.
cards.searchQuery: silver chloride dissolves in ammonia complex ion formation solubility

cards.title: $K_{sp}(\ce{Mg(OH)2}) = 5.6 \times 10^{-12}$. What is the pH of a saturated solution at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, to two decimals?
cards.body:
10.35

$K_{sp} = 4s^3$, so $s = (1.4 \times 10^{-12})^{1/3} = 1.1 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{M}$.

Then $[\ce{OH-}] = 2s = 2.2 \times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{M}$, $\mathrm{pOH} = 3.65$ and $\mathrm{pH} = 10.35$.

Watch out: the hydroxide concentration is $2s$, not $s$.
cards.searchQuery: pH of saturated magnesium hydroxide solution from Ksp

cards.title: A mixture has $Q > K$. In which direction does the net reaction proceed?
cards.body:
reverse

There are too many products relative to equilibrium, so products are consumed and reactants form until $Q$ falls to $K$.

Key idea: compare $Q$ with $K$. If $Q > K$ go left; if $Q < K$ go right.
cards.searchQuery: reaction quotient Q greater than K reverse direction
